Ancestral Property Partition (Anshabanda) in Nepal: Law, Rights, and Disputes

📅 Published: 2025-05-01
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 9 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

Ancestral property partition (Anshabanda / अंशबण्डा) under Part 3, Chapter 10 of the Muluki Civil Code 2074 is the legal process of dividing family estate (Paitrik Sampatti) equally among lawful co-heirs (Anshiyar). Under current law, father, mother, husband, wife, sons, and daughters hold equal co-ownership rights. If co-heirs cannot agree on an amicable registered partition deed, any co-heir can institute a formal Partition Suit (Anshabanda Mudda) in District Court to compel equitable property distribution.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Father, mother, sons, and daughters hold equal coparcenary rights under Section 205.
  • Self-acquired property (Swaparjita Sampatti) is exempt from family partition.
  • Concealing ancestral assets during partition constitutes an offense resulting in forfeiture of the hidden asset.

In Nepalese civil litigation, Anshabanda (अंशबण्डा) disputes dominate District Court dockets. Dividing ancestral holdings among multiple generations involves reconciling ancient family traditions with modern statutory equal-rights principles established under the Muluki Civil Code 2074.

1. Who is an Anshiyar? (Equal Statutory Coparceners)

Under Section 205 of the Civil Code, the statutory co-heirs entitled to equal shares in ancestral estate are: Father, Mother, Husband, Wife, Sons, and Daughters. Modern law eliminates historic gender discrimination: married and unmarried daughters share identical coparcenary rights with sons.

2. Ancestral Estate vs. Self-Acquired Property

A crucial legal distinction governs what property is subject to partition:

  • Ancestral Property (पैतृक सम्पत्ति): Assets inherited from parents, grandparents, or acquired through the utilization of ancestral capital. This property must be partitioned equally among all co-heirs.
  • Self-Acquired Property (स्वआर्जित सम्पत्ति): Assets earned solely through an individual personal skill, employment, private business, or personal gift. Under Section 208, self-acquired property belongs exclusively to the earner and is completely exempt from partition claims.

3. Penalties for Concealing Assets (Jiyajatha Dhanteko)

Co-heirs often attempt to hide prime plots or bank accounts from siblings during partition. Under Section 218 of the Civil Code, if an heir deliberately conceals ancestral assets when submitting the property inventory to the court, the concealed asset is confiscated and divided exclusively among the other honest co-heirs—the concealing party receives zero share of that asset.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 205 (Equal Share in Property) Equal partition rights of father, mother, sons, and daughters.
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 218 (Concealment of Property) Heir who conceals ancestral property forfeits rights to the concealed property.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Genealogical Family Tree (Bansawali) verified by local ward office
  • ✔ Ward Family Relationship Certificate (Nata Pramanit Pramanpatra)
  • ✔ Lalpurjas and cadastral blue prints of all ancestral properties
  • ✔ Citizenship Certificates of all co-heirs

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can parents refuse to partition ancestral property to their adult children?

Under Section 207, any adult co-heir has a legal right to demand their partition share at any time. If family elders refuse, the heir can file a formal Partition Suit (Anshabanda Mudda) in District Court to compel division.
